notes.4: Only a few candidates had problems with this question. The most common error was to choose the response in which the mass was smallest without considering the effect of volume.
notes.6: Most candidates understood that an object is in equilibrium if both the resultant force acting on it and the resultant moment on it are zero.
notes.10: Most candidates showed a good understanding of the work done when different loads are move through different distances.
notes.15: Only stronger candidates appeared to recognise the term ‘heat capacity’. Candidates should be encouraged to familiarise themselves with basic terminology.
notes.16: Most candidates were able to identify the materials from which the pan was made, showing that there was a good practical understanding of conduction.
notes.18: Some candidates did not read the question carefully enough. The question asked which row in the table did not show a correct unit for the quantity in the left-hand column. The symbol λ does not represent a unit, it is merely used to label an unknown wavelength.
notes.20: Many candidates recognised that total internal reflection did not occur in the example, but others were unable to identify the angle of incidence of a light ray striking the surface of a glass block.
notes.21: Most candidates were able to recognise the reversed image that is seen in a plane mirror.
notes.22: Candidates needed to read this question carefully. The basic physics that was needed to answer the question successfully was that all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed in a vacuum and a knowledge of the wavelengths of different types of electromagnetic wave.
notes.25: Most candidates were aware that iron is the only magnetic material in the given list
notes.28: Only stronger candidates answered this well. The circuit is a form of potentiometer, the current is the same in both resistors and therefore (using V = I R ) the potential difference across the 2.0 Ω is twice that across the 1.0 Ω resistor. The total potential difference across the two resistors is the sum of the potential differences across the two resistors which is 18 V.
notes.32: Most candidates thought that the total resistance of two resistors in parallel is equal to the average of the two resistances rather than it being smaller than either resistor. The logic is that the charge carriers now have a choice of paths to take, meaning that more charge carriers can pass per unit time.
notes.37: Only stronger candidates showed understanding of the α -scattering experiment. Candidates needed to know that a small proportion of the α -particles are repelled by the nucleus and that the electric charge in the nucleus is produced by the protons in the nucleus.
notes.39: Only stronger candidates used the information about the half-life of the isotope that was given. If the term half-life was understood, then candidates knew that the count rate would have fallen to half the initial rate after six hours and that after another six hours it would have fallen to half again, i.e., a quarter of the initial count. Graph C should have been identifiable as the only possible graph.
